items.title: American podiatrist leaving Nova Scotia over bureaucratic frustrations
items.description: A U.S. podiatrist says he is leaving the province because his patients have to wait years to see a surgeon for procedures on their feet, even though he's trained to do the procedures in his clinic.

items.title: Ontario extending transit fare integration program by 2 years
items.description: Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria announced the extension of OneFare, which the government says saves transit users up to $1,600 per year, on Monday.

items.title: Ford government takes over northern Ontario school board
items.description: A ministry report in October outlined what it called overwhelming dysfunction at the Near North District School Board and suggested ministry intervention.

items.title: Vancouver International Black Film Festival returns for its fifth edition
items.description: A hybrid lineup of films, panels, and workshops spotlights creators from Canada and around the world.

items.title: Northern B.C. bitcoin mines are transitioning into AI data centres
items.description: Iren, the company behind major data centres in northern B.C. is converting its infrastructure from bitcoin mining into AI storage. The Australia-based company is upgrading equipment at its sites in Prince George, Mackenzie and Canal Flats sites.

items.title: Montreal museum spotlights sex workers history of activism and resistance
items.description: When community group Mile End Chavurah held an event in 2023 to name Jewish Montreal's "new patron saint," Maimie Pinzer was the winning choice.

items.title: The Culinary Commons helps Vancouver chefs gather
items.description: 1250 East Georgia Street is serving Vancouver's culinary community. ]

items.title: Nova Scotia begins sell off of U.S. booze, plans to donate proceeds to charity
items.description: Nova Scotia liquor stores will once again stock booze from the United States beginning today, but for a limited time only.

items.title: All of Toronto's speed cameras are gone. How did we get to this point?
items.description: Toronto's speed cameras may be gone, but this time there are no mysterious vandals wielding power tools, no blurry suspect photos and no police investigation.
